name: sacrifice

attributes.attribute: the offering of one thing to gain another among the Celts
a neck ring sometimes twisted out of shape before being offered

sources: Hull, Eleanor. Folklore of the British Isles. (London: Methuen & Co., Ltd., 1928), 157.
Wait, G. A. Ritual and Religion in Iron Age Britain. Bar British Series 149(i) (Oxford: 1985), 122+.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Sacrifice is a cosmological concept. The Celts offered one thing to gain another, as most peoples did. They gave goods to their gods at set times and in times of danger. A person damaged an object before the offering. The Celts worshiped outdoors, so they left the gift in a natural place. They smashed a piece of jewelry or bent a torc out of shape. Then they threw it into a lake or buried it in a bog. An animal might be killed. Sometimes the whole beast burned so no part fed a human. At other times they offered the best meat and ate the rest in a feast. Some writers tie sacrifice to what was once alive. Offerings were things never alive, such as coins and jewelry. In common use, sacrifice names anything given to the gods and placed beyond human use.

okr.objective: Document sacrifice as a Celtic cosmological practice.
